content: {"summary":"This lecture introduces what computation means in Python by distinguishing syntax from semantics and by explaining how programs are built from objects, expressions, and assignments. It emphasizes that a computer executes only the instructions given, so a program has one meaning even when that meaning differs from the programmer's intent, and it previews control flow as the next topic.","key_points":["Syntax concerns whether an expression is well formed, while semantics concerns its meaning: an expression like adding a word to a number can be syntactically correct (operator, operand, operator) but semantically meaningless, and in English a syntactically and semantically correct phrase such as \"flying planes can be dangerous\" can have more than one meaning, whereas a program has only one meaning because the computer only does what you tell it to do.","Errors in Python fall into categories: syntax errors are easily caught by Python and point to the exact incorrect line; static semantic errors can also be caught by Python as long as the program has gone down the branch where the error happens; and the most frustrating case, especially when starting out, is when the program does something different from what was expected, such as outputting 10 instead of 0, because it simply executed the program as written, and programs might also crash (stop running) or fail to stop, both of which can be fixed by returning to the code.","Python programs are sequences of definitions and commands: expressions are evaluated, commands tell the interpreter to do something, and commands can be typed directly in the shell on the right for simple testing or written in the editor on the left as longer, more complicated programs.","In Python everything is an object, and every object has a type that determines the operations that can be done on it; objects are either scalar, meaning basic and unable to be subdivided, such as the number five, or non-scalar, meaning they have internal structure, such as the list 5, 6, 7, 8, which can be subdivided into a sequence of numbers.","The scalar objects in Python are integers (whole numbers), floats (real numbers, anything with a decimal), Booleans (Bools, with only the two values True and False, capitalized), and NoneType (with only the one value None, representing the absence of a type); the type command returns an object's type, and conversion places the target type before the object, so float(3) converts integer 3 to float 3.0, while converting to an integer truncates by removing the decimal and what follows it rather than rounding.","Printing is how a program interacts with the user: typing 3 plus 2 in the shell shows the value 5 only as a peek for the programmer, but running 3 plus 2 in the editor prints nothing, so the print command is needed to actually print the value 5 to the console; an \"Out\" in the shell indicates an interaction within the shell only, while no \"Out\" means it was printed to the console.","Expressions combine objects and operators and evaluate to a value, with syntax object-operator-object; for addition, subtraction, and multiplication the result type depends on the operands (integer if both are integers, float if at least one is a float), division always produces a float regardless of operands, the percent sign gives the remainder when dividing i by j, and the star star operator raises i to the power of j, with the usual mathematical precedence and parentheses available to override it.","Assignment uses the equal sign to bind a name on the left to a value on the right, storing the value in memory so it can be accessed later by typing the name; names should be descriptive, and naming expressions allows reuse of names instead of values and makes code look nicer, as in a circle-area program that assigns pi to 3.14159 and radius to 2.2 and then assigns area to an expression referring to pi and radius, whose values are looked up in memory and substituted.","Unlike math, where you can solve for x with things on both sides of the equal sign, in programming the right-hand side is always an expression evaluated to a value and the left-hand side is always a single variable, so to solve for x you must tell the computer exactly how; variable names can be rebound by new assignment statements, as when radius is bound to 2.2 and then radius = radius + 1 takes away the binding to 2.2, computes 3.2, and rebinds that value to radius, leaving 2.2 in memory with no handle to retrieve it until the garbage collector may reuse it, and importantly the value of area does not change because the computer was never told to recalculate it."]}
